source.title: How much do language models memorize?
source.authors: J. X. Morris; Chawin Sitawarin; Chuan Guo; Narine Kokhlikyan; G. Suh; Alexander M. Rush; Kamalika Chaudhuri; Saeed Mahloujifar

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices
record.tranche_reason: The study measures memorization and generalization in synthetic sequences and text with GPT-style language models, extending related questions to language modeling. Its experiments do not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports model capacity, text memorization, train/test loss, extraction, and membership inference. Rows below cover outcomes relevant to the broader memorization–generalization relationship. Membership-inference results are omitted because they measure attack performance rather than the generalization gap or a property mapped in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures compression-based memorization, capacity, text loss and extraction in transformers, but none of V1–V8. Random-sequence fitting is not the random-label versus natural-label comparison in V1; varying dataset size relative to capacity is not the post-interpolation width intervention in V2. Related findings in a new setting alone do not establish T3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' interpretation. They propose a compression-based definition separating unintended memorization from generalization, estimate transformer capacity, relate dataset-to-capacity ratios to double descent, and develop membership-inference scaling laws validated on larger models. Their practical compression measurements are approximations, and synthetic capacity estimates are lower bounds; the suggested explanation of double descent is not established causally.
record.recipe_differences: Uses compression-based estimates of memorization and language-model loss, rather than the classification architectures, interventions, and measures in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured outcomes vary with model size, dataset size, reference model, and precision. The authors state that results need not generalize to other datasets, architectures, or training setups.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-sequence memorization saturates at an empirical capacity; mean estimates are 3.51 bits per parameter in bfloat16 and 3.83 in fp32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested GPT-style transformers have a finite empirically measured random-sequence storage capacity that increases modestly with training precision.

fits_no_version.finding: Sample-level unintended memorization varies with model size, dataset size and reference model, and can decline as text generalization improves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compression-based unintended memorization in the tested text models depends on capacity, dataset scale and the reference used to separate generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report dataset-size double descent near estimated capacity and near-convergence of training and test extraction rates at large dataset sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these transformer experiments, dataset size relative to estimated capacity predicts test-loss behavior, and successful extraction need not distinguish training data from held-out data.

record.problems: The authors state that results are specific to their experimental environment and may not generalize to other datasets, architectures, or training setups. Synthetic-data capacity is described as a lower bound because gradient descent may not find global optima. Several trends are presented in figures without separate numeric values for each model and condition.
record.rows_left_out: Membership-inference attack scores and scaling-law validation results (Sections 5 and 5.2; Figures 7, 9, and 14; Table 2) were left out because they report attack performance rather than the generalization gap or a property mapped in the versions. Extraction results at other prefix lengths are not separately extracted because the result text supplied here does not give their individual values.

untested.parts: No comparison of fixed random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy using the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level evaluation under random labels.
No width sweep measuring test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison or tuning intervention.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted training recipes.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking against generalization gaps.
No removal of examples selected by inclusion-based memorization and comparison with random removal after retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because the rows measure different constructs or interventions; this does not deny their reported findings. No additional unrecorded result in the supplied text directly tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment compares fitting random labels with generalizing on natural labels.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; dataset size and model capacity are varied in GPT-style language models instead.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD for held-out performance.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers
rows.size_stated: 1–8 layers; hidden dimensions 32 to 512; 100K to 20M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured unintended memorization on uniformly sampled synthetic sequences across dataset sizes.
rows.measure: Total unintended memorization in bits across dataset sizes
rows.value: Small datasets are completely memorized by all models with enough capacity; memorization plateaus once a model reaches its capacity.
rows.note: The paper describes the pattern across models and dataset sizes; it does not give a separate numeric value for each model in the supplied result text.
rows.check: Measures random-sequence memorization capacity, not V1's label comparison. Training duration is 10^6 steps, not 106. The reported plateau and complete memorization of sufficiently small datasets are supported.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers, fp32 and bfloat16
rows.operation_detail: Compared estimated memorization capacity per parameter at two training precisions.
rows.measure: Mean capacity in bits per parameter
rows.uncertainty: ±0.1, as stated for the table means
rows.locator: Table 1; Section 3.2, “How does precision affect capacity?”
rows.note: The authors describe this as a small increase, far less than the 2x increase in parameter bit precision.
rows.check: The capacity means of 3.83 versus 3.51 bits per parameter are supported, but precision-dependent storage capacity measures no listed version.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers trained on FineWeb text
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and model size, then measured sample-level unintended memorization.

conditions.value: large oracle model trained on the full data distribution

rows.value: It increases with model parameters and decreases with training-set size; with an oracle reference, it increases as the smaller model learns more about a small training set, then decreases as it generalizes.
rows.note: The text gives trends across model and dataset sizes without separate numeric values for each model-condition pair.
rows.check: Compression-based sample memorization is distinct from V1's random-label comparison and V8's inclusion-based memorization and removal intervention. Section 4 supports the trends; Figure 4 shows train/test loss rather than directly plotting unintended memorization. Distinguish the equal-size reference from the higher-capacity oracle reference.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers trained on FineWeb text
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured train and evaluation losses.
rows.measure: Train and test loss; evaluation performance
rows.value: Evaluation loss begins to decrease once capacity is reached; evaluation performance decreases as training-set size nears model capacity, then rapidly drops as dataset capacity exceeds model capacity.
rows.locator: Section 4, “Dataset-to-capacity ratio predicts double descent”; Figures 3 and 4
rows.note: This varies dataset size relative to estimated capacity, not width alone. The authors call the observed evaluation pattern double descent.
rows.check: Dataset-size sweeps do not test V2's width intervention. The value repeats internally confusing source wording: a drop in evaluation loss means improved performance. Record the authors' claimed nonmonotonic test-loss pattern and subsequent loss decrease beyond capacity without describing both phases as declining performance. Figure 3 concerns synthetic data; Figure 4 concerns text.

rows.subject: GPT-style transformers trained on FineWeb text
rows.operation_detail: Compared exact extraction rates on training and non-overlapping evaluation samples as dataset size increased.
rows.value: At sufficiently large dataset sizes, the training extraction rate converges to nearly exactly the test extraction rate.
rows.locator: Section 4, “Generalization explains nonzero extraction rates”; Figure 17
rows.note: The authors attribute successful extraction at large dataset sizes to generalization.
rows.check: Train/test extraction convergence measures none of the versions. The extraction figure is Figure 8; Section 4's reference to Figure 17 is erroneous because Figure 17 shows membership-inference scaling. Near-equal extraction rates support the authors' population-level interpretation, rather than proving the cause of every extracted training sequence.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
